_comment: GENERATED BY MATUGEN - do not edit by hand. Template: ~/.config/matugen/templates/quickshell-colors.json
_policy: Two axes, and they are the same two every other application in this setup follows: SURFACES, TEXT and OUTLINES come from the scheme (the ui_* roles, fixed for as long as the scheme is) and ACCENTS come from the wallpaper (the Material 3 roles, regenerated on every change). The shell used to be the one exception -- its surfaces followed the image as well -- and the header of Theme.qml still argues for that exception. The argument was sound while the alternative was a base fixed at Tokyo Night forever: M3 guarantees the contrast of each role PAIR whatever the wallpaper is, which was worth more than a base nobody could change. It is not worth more than the base the user picked. desktop-scheme moves the background of GTK, Qt, kitty and zathura and used to leave the shell's alone, so choosing a scheme changed the whole desktop except the part of it this repository draws. The pairing rule itself still holds and still matters -- on_surface over surface, on_primary over primary, never a hardcoded hex over a generated one -- but on this side of the fence the pairs are the scheme's, and a scheme is contrast-checked once, by hand, when it is written, instead of per wallpaper by M3.
_surface_ladder: M3 wants four surface levels and no scheme has four names for them in the same place. Counted in schemes/README.md section 4.3: BELOW the window Tokyo Night has five steps, Catppuccin three and Gruvbox two -- but ABOVE it all three have exactly four, and it is the four above that this ladder needs. So `surface` is the window itself and the three containers climb the raised tones: ui_bg -> ui_bg_raised -> ui_bevel_midlight -> ui_border. That is base/surface0/surface1/surface2 in Catppuccin and bg0/bg1/bg2/bg3 in Gruvbox, i.e. each scheme's own ladder, unbent. ui_bg_button, ui_bg_control and ui_selection_disabled are deliberately NOT used: all three collapse onto ui_bg_raised in Catppuccin and Gruvbox, so a ladder built on them would spend two M3 levels on one hex and leave a card invisible against the card behind it. ui_bevel_midlight rather than ui_border_dim at level 3 for the same reason in reverse -- the two are one colour in Catppuccin and in Gruvbox, and in Tokyo Night midlight (#363b54) stands further off ui_border than border_dim (#3b4261) does. Cross-check: the fb_* fallbacks in every scheme file, which were filled independently, agree with this ladder in 11 of their 12 cells; the twelfth is Tokyo Night's fb_surface_container_high (#343a52), two levels off ui_bevel_midlight.
_outlines: The two outline roles cannot come out of that ladder, because the four surfaces already spend four of the five tones each scheme has above its window. `outline` takes ui_text_muted, which sits one step above every surface level in all three schemes -- and which is what the shell actually paints with it: Theme.outline is a TEXT colour far more often than a border (the placeholder in SearchField.qml, a muted line in AudioPage.qml, an undescribed bind in KeybindsPage.qml), and 'placeholder text, present but not readable as content' is ui_text_muted's definition word for word. `outline_variant` takes ui_border_dim, a divider, which is what it is drawn as everywhere. ONE collision is left and it is the cheap one: ui_border_dim and ui_bevel_midlight are the same tone in Catppuccin and Gruvbox, so an outline_variant border on surface_container_high melts into its own fill. Two sites do that (modules/settings/SettingsSection.qml:90 and modules/settings/pages/UpdatesPage.qml:560) and in both the fill is the HOVER state of a pill that is transparent at rest, so the pill still reads against the card behind it. The alternative -- outline_variant on ui_border -- collides with surface_container_highest instead, which is the ground under seven outline_variant borders including every tooltip, and in all three schemes rather than two.
_alerts: ON THIS SIDE OF THE FENCE, and the distinction is the whole point. An alert must not follow the WALLPAPER: amber is 'watch out' and red is 'something is wrong' whatever image is on screen, and M3's error role is derived from the image, so over a red picture a critical reading would come out the hue of the rest of the bar. That argument is untouched -- see `_no_error_role` below, which is why this file still passes no error/on_error through. What it never meant is 'hardcoded'. A scheme is not a wallpaper: it is chosen by hand and it moves only when the user moves it, so an alert taken from a scheme is as fixed as anything on screen is. GTK, Qt and zathura have painted their alerts from sem_* since the templates were substituted; the shell was the last surface on the desktop still showing Tokyo Night amber and red on a Gruvbox base, and these three keys are what ends that. MEASURED UNDER ALL THREE SCHEMES against all four surface levels, and it is not all one way: warning improves everywhere (worst pair 3.26 -> 3.84 on Gruvbox, 3.34 -> 5.25 on Catppuccin), Tokyo Night does not move because the literals were its scheme, and Gruvbox's critical gets WORSE -- #fb4934 is darker than #f7768e, so on surface_container_highest (#665c54, Gruvbox's own bg3) it falls 2.46:1 to 1.89:1. The weak pairing is Gruvbox's red on Gruvbox's bg3, it is weak in every application here and not only in the shell, and it is fixed in schemes/gruvbox-dark.json if it is worth fixing. The long version is in Theme.qml, where the readers are.
_alerts_not_emitted: sem_on_warning and sem_success are filled by every scheme and are deliberately NOT here, for the reason `_no_error_role` records: a key nothing reads is a colour written into the void. THERE IS NO textOnWarning BECAUSE THERE IS NOWHERE TO PAINT IT. All 24 sites that touch Theme.warning were classified: every one is a foreground -- a Text, a Nerd Font glyph, a border, a meter tick, a slider fill with nothing on it -- or a Qt.alpha() tint of 0.16 to 0.22 over a card, and on none of those four tints does anything switch to an on-warning ink -- what sits on them is either textOnSurface or the amber itself. Not one solid amber ground in the tree carries readable content. Theme.textOnCritical, by contrast, has four real sites, all the same shape: hovering a Forget button fills it solid red and flips the glyph (NetworkPage.qml:524, BluetoothPage.qml:548, Island.qml:952). It would also be a duplicate key: sem_on_warning and sem_on_critical are the same hex in all three schemes. AND THERE IS NO success BECAUSE THE SHELL HAS NO 'IT WORKED' COLOUR AT ALL: no green hex exists anywhere in the QML tree, and the states that would want one -- an `ok` update verdict, a connected network, a paired device, a charging battery -- are painted Theme.primary today. Giving them a green is a design change with its own argument to make, and it has to happen on the drawing side first; this key would follow it, not lead it. Both roles stay in the vocabulary because GTK consumes them. Add either key here on the day a reader appears in Theme.qml, in the same change.
_accents: Below this line nothing changed and nothing should: these nine are the wallpaper's half of the desktop, derived by matugen from the image on every change, and they are why Theme.qml reads this file through a watching FileView instead of being generated as QML. They keep their M3 pairing among themselves -- on_primary is only ever painted on primary, on_primary_container only on primary_container -- because that pairing is the only contrast guarantee an accent has.
_no_error_role: M3 has error/on_error and this file used to emit them, and Theme.qml read neither: it held `warning` and `critical` as literals instead, because an alert tinted by the wallpaper loses the one thing it is for. So the two lines wrote a colour nothing could consume, and they went. The alerts have a source now -- the scheme's sem_* roles, above -- and it is still not this one: error/on_error stay out because they are derived per image, which is the fault, not because the shell has nothing to paint red with. THE RULE THE PARAGRAPH IS REALLY FOR is the one that outlived its example: every key in this file is read by exactly one property in Theme.qml, and every such property reads a key. Keep it that way. If some role really is wanted, add the reader in the same change.
